title: The metallic bond
html:
Guiding question

What determines the metallic nature and properties of an element?

Start with what you already know. Think of a copper wire, a steel bridge, a gold ring and an aluminium can. Between them they show almost every typical metal property: metals are strong and hard, have high melting and boiling points, conduct electricity and conduct heat, are malleable (can be hammered into shape), ductile (can be stretched into wires), lustrous (shiny) and sonorous (ring when struck). This topic explains all of them with one model.

Metals sit on the left and in the centre of the periodic table. Their atoms have low ionization energies and low electronegativities, so they lose their outer (valence) electrons easily. In a piece of metal, those valence electrons are not owned by any one atom. They spread through the whole structure. This one idea explains almost every property of metals in this topic.

S2.3.1 The metallic bond

Metals are giant crystalline lattices

Metal atoms pack closely together, layer upon layer, in a regular repeating pattern: a giant lattice. Each atom releases its valence electrons into the structure. This leaves a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) surrounded by a "sea" of delocalized electrons that are free to move through the whole lattice.

Because the particles are arranged regularly, metals are crystalline. The crystals (grains) are usually too small to see, but sometimes you can see them, for example the large, shiny zinc crystals ("spangles") on the surface of a galvanised lamp post. Silver crystals can also be grown in the lab by placing a copper wire in silver nitrate solution: the copper displaces the silver, which grows as branching, glittering crystals on the wire.

DefinitionA metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) and a sea of delocalized electrons.
  • Delocalized means the electrons are not tied to one atom or one bond. They are mobile and shared by all the cations in the lattice.
  • Only the valence electrons are delocalized. Core (inner-shell) electrons stay bound to their own ion.
  • The attraction acts in all directions, so metallic bonding is non-directional. This matters for malleability and for alloys (S2.4).
  • The structure as a whole is neutral: the total positive charge on the cations equals the total negative charge of the delocalized electrons.

A metallic lattice looks a little like an ionic lattice, since both are giant regular arrays held by electrostatic attraction. The difference is that in an ionic lattice the negative charge sits on fixed anions, while in a metal it is spread out in mobile electrons. A useful summary: delocalized electrons are mobile electrons.

Which of the following is the best description of delocalized electrons in metallic bonding?

  1. Core electrons that can move freely between metal ions
  2. Valence electrons that can move freely between metal ions
  3. Core and valence electrons that can move freely between metal ions
  4. Valence electrons bound to metal ions

Only the outer (valence) electrons are released into the lattice, and "delocalized" means they move freely between the ions. Core electrons stay bound to their own ion, and electrons bound to particular ions are by definition not delocalized.

Common mistakeDo not describe a metal as "positive ions and negative ions" or as "atoms sharing electron pairs". There are no anions and no localized bonds. Also, do not say the electrons are "free" without saying they are delocalized valence electrons. Examiners expect both the cation lattice and the delocalized electrons in a description.
Write your own description of a metallic bond (with a labelled diagram in mind), then reveal a model answer

Metals have giant structures of closely packed atoms in a regular pattern; the crystals we sometimes see on metal surfaces are evidence of this. Each atom loses its outer-shell (valence) electrons, which become delocalized and are free to move through the whole structure. The resulting positive ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction to this sea of delocalized electrons. A labelled diagram should show rows of "+" cations with "e⁻" scattered between them, labelled metal cation and delocalized electron.

Which particles are present in solid magnesium?

  1. Mg atoms sharing pairs of electrons
  2. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions
  3. Mg²⁺ ions and delocalized electrons
  4. Mg⁺ ions and Mg⁻ ions

Magnesium (2 valence electrons) gives Mg²⁺ cations in a sea of delocalized electrons, two per atom. There are no anions in a pure metal and no localized electron-pair bonds.

title: Properties of metals and their uses
html:
Properties of metals explained

Every property in the list from the start of the topic follows from the model of cations in a sea of delocalized electrons. Learn the explanation, not just the property.

PropertyExplanation using the metallic model
Electrical conductivity (solid and liquid)Delocalized electrons are mobile charge carriers. When a potential difference is applied, they move through the lattice towards the positive terminal.
Thermal conductivityWhen one end is heated, the delocalized electrons there gain kinetic energy. They move quickly through the lattice and pass the energy on by colliding with other electrons and ions. Vibrating, closely packed cations also pass energy on. Insulators have no delocalized electrons, so they cannot transfer heat this way.
Malleability and ductilityThe bonding is non-directional. When a force is applied, layers of cations slide over one another but stay surrounded by the electron sea, so the attraction remains and the metal does not shatter. (In an ionic lattice, sliding brings like charges next to each other, and the crystal shatters.)
High melting and boiling points (most metals)Many strong electrostatic attractions act between the cations and the delocalized electrons throughout the giant lattice. A lot of energy is needed to overcome them.
LustreDelocalized electrons absorb and re-emit light of many frequencies, so freshly cut metal surfaces look shiny.
High density (most metals)The ions are closely packed in the lattice.

Malleability: why a hammer blow does not shatter a metal

Picture a hammer hitting a block of metal. The layers of identical cations are pushed along and simply move to the next position in the layer below. At every point they are still surrounded by delocalized electrons, so the attractive forces are never lost. The metal changes shape instead of breaking. Contrast this with an ionic crystal: a small shift lines up cation next to cation and anion next to anion, the repulsion splits the crystal, and it is brittle.

Why are metals malleable while ionic solids are brittle?

  1. Metals have weaker bonds, so the layers break more easily
  2. Metal atoms are smaller than ions
  3. Metals contain no electrostatic forces
  4. Metallic bonding is non-directional, so cation layers can slide and stay attracted to the delocalized electrons

The key word is non-directional. After the layers slide, the cations are still surrounded by the electron sea, so no repulsion builds up. Metallic bonds are not weak, and they are electrostatic.

Exam tipFor conduction, name the charge carrier. In metals and in the wires of a circuit the current is carried by delocalized electrons. In a molten or dissolved ionic compound (the electrolyte) it is carried by mobile ions.

Electrical resistance and temperature

Metals are not perfect conductors. Resistance comes from the moving delocalized electrons colliding with the cations in the lattice. When the temperature rises, the cations vibrate more, so the electrons collide with them more often. Resistance therefore increases with temperature for metals.

Predict: a metal wire is cooled in liquid nitrogen. What happens to its resistance? Then reveal

The resistance decreases. The cations vibrate less, so the delocalized electrons collide with them less often and flow more easily.

Relating properties to uses

The syllabus asks you to link the properties of a metal to what it is used for. Always give the property and the reason it matters.

MetalUseRelevant properties
CopperElectrical wiring, cooking pansExcellent electrical and thermal conductor; ductile; quite unreactive
AluminiumAircraft bodies, overhead power cables, foil, drinks cansLow density; good conductor; malleable; resists corrosion because of its protective oxide layer
Iron (as steel)Bridges, buildings, car bodiesStrong, hard, cheap; can be pressed into shape
TungstenFilament lamps, welding electrodesVery high melting point (about 3400 °C)
Gold, silverJewellery, electrical contactsLustrous; very unreactive (does not tarnish or corrode); excellent conductor
TitaniumHip replacements, aircraft enginesStrong, low density, corrosion resistant, high melting point

Transition metals are often used for furnaces, jet engines and construction because they are strong, conduct heat well and have high melting points.

Overhead power cables are made of aluminium (with a steel core) rather than copper, even though copper conducts better. Which property of aluminium is most important here?

  1. Low density
  2. High melting point
  3. Lustre
  4. Sonority

Cables hang between pylons over long distances, so their mass matters. Aluminium is a good conductor with a much lower density than copper, and its oxide layer protects it from corrosion.

Plenary: explain (1) heat conduction, (2) electrical conduction and (3) malleability in metals. Try it, then reveal
  1. Heat: delocalized electrons gain kinetic energy where the metal is heated and carry it rapidly through the lattice by collisions; vibrating cations also pass energy along.
  2. Electricity: delocalized electrons are mobile charged particles that drift towards the positive terminal when a potential difference is applied.
  3. Malleability: layers of cations slide over one another; the non-directional attraction to the delocalized electrons is kept, so the metal changes shape without breaking.

title: Strength of the metallic bond
html:
S2.3.2 Strength of the metallic bond

The strength of a metallic bond depends on how strongly the cations attract the delocalized electrons. Three linked factors control it:

  1. Charge on the cation: a higher charge attracts the electron sea more strongly.
  2. Number of delocalized electrons per atom: this usually equals the ionic charge (Na gives 1, Mg gives 2, Al gives 3), so more electrons go with a higher charge.
  3. Radius of the cation: a smaller ion lets the delocalized electrons get closer to the nucleus, so the attraction is stronger.
Key pointMetallic bonds are strongest when the cations have a high charge and a small radius (a high charge density). A stronger metallic bond means a higher melting point, a higher boiling point and a higher enthalpy of atomization.

In one sentence: the greater the charge density of the cation, the stronger the metallic bond.

Trend down a group: group 1

MetalLiNaKRbCs
Melting point / °C18198633929

All group 1 ions have a 1+ charge and give one delocalized electron each. Going down the group, the ionic radius increases because there are more occupied electron shells. The delocalized electrons are further from the nucleus of each cation, so the charge density falls and the electrostatic attraction gets weaker. Less energy is needed to overcome it, so the melting point decreases down the group. Lithium has the strongest metallic bond in group 1.

Li, Na and K all form 1+ ions. Which has the strongest metallic bonding?

  1. Li
  2. Na
  3. K
  4. All the same, because the charge is the same

With equal charge, size decides. Li⁺ is the smallest ion, so the delocalized electrons are closest to its nucleus: highest charge density, strongest attraction, highest melting point (181 °C).

Exam tipA common question compares group 1 (melting points decrease down the group) with group 17 (melting points increase down the group). For group 1, talk about larger ions and weaker attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons. For group 17, talk about more electrons and stronger London (dispersion) forces between the X₂ molecules. Do not explain the group 1 trend using attraction between the nucleus and its own valence electron: the markscheme does not accept this.

Trend across a period: Na, Mg, Al

MetalNaMgAl
IonNa⁺Mg²⁺Al³⁺
Delocalized electrons per atom123
Ionic radius / pm1027254
Melting point / °C98650660
Boiling point / °C88310902519
Explain the trend in melting and boiling points from Na to Al before you read on, then reveal

The positive charge on the ion gets larger and there are more delocalized electrons per atom, so the electrostatic attraction is greater. At the same time the ions get smaller. A stronger bond needs more energy to separate the particles, so a higher temperature is needed.

From Na to Al the ionic charge rises (1+ → 2+ → 3+), the number of delocalized electrons rises, and the ionic radius falls. Each change strengthens the attraction between the cations and the electron sea, so more energy is needed to separate the particles and the melting and boiling points increase.

Melting point depends partly on the crystal structure as well, which is why Mg and Al melt at almost the same temperature. The boiling point shows the trend in bond strength more clearly, because boiling separates the particles completely.

Worked example

Question: Explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium. [3]

  1. Both have metallic bonding: a lattice of cations attracted to delocalized electrons.
  2. Mg forms Mg²⁺ (2 delocalized electrons per atom); Na forms Na⁺ (1 delocalized electron per atom). Mg²⁺ is also smaller than Na⁺.
  3. Mg²⁺ has a higher charge density, so the electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons is stronger, and more energy is needed to overcome it.

Which metal would you expect to have the highest boiling point?

  1. Na
  2. K
  3. Al
  4. Mg

Al³⁺ has the highest charge, gives three delocalized electrons per atom, and is the smallest ion of the four, so its metallic bonding is strongest (boiling point 2519 °C).

Using the table, by how many degrees is the boiling point of Al higher than that of Na?

2519 − 883 = 1636 °C. Compare the melting points (660 − 98 = 562 °C): the boiling points show the bond-strength trend much more clearly.
Common mistakeMetals do not melt because "bonds between atoms break". In a molten metal the metallic bonding still exists, because the liquid still conducts. Melting only gives the cations enough energy to move past one another. In boiling, the particles separate completely.

Mercury (melting point −39 °C) is the well-known exception: it is a liquid metal at room temperature, so metals do not always have high melting points.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • "Describe metallic bonding." [2] Name the lattice of positive ions/cations ✓ and the electrostatic attraction to a sea of delocalized electrons ✓.
  • "Explain why metals are malleable." [2] Layers of cations can slide over each other ✓ and the non-directional attraction to the delocalized electrons is kept, so the metal does not break ✓.
  • "Which has the strongest metallic bond?" Pick the cation with the highest charge and smallest radius (Li in group 1; Al from Na/Mg/Al).
  • "Explain why the resistance of metals increases with temperature." [2] Lattice ions vibrate more ✓, so collisions between the delocalized electrons and the cations are more frequent ✓.
  • AHL "Explain the high melting point of transition metals." Both 3d and 4s electrons are delocalized ✓, so there are more delocalized electrons, with higher charge and smaller ions, and a stronger electrostatic attraction ✓.
Plenary: explain the difference in metallic bond strength between Li and K, and between Na and Al. Then reveal

Li vs K: same charge (1+), but Li⁺ is much smaller, so the delocalized electrons are closer to the nucleus and attracted more strongly; Li has the stronger bond.

Na vs Al: Al³⁺ has a higher charge, gives three delocalized electrons rather than one, and is smaller than Na⁺; Al has the much stronger bond.

title: Transition elements and delocalized d-electrons (AHL)
html:
S2.3.3 Transition elements and delocalized d-electrons AHL

Starter: write down the properties of transition metals that you already know. Typical answers: high melting points; good conductors of heat and electricity (so they are used for furnaces and jet engines); strong (so they are used for construction).

Transition elements, such as Ti, Cr, Fe and W, have unusually high melting points, high densities, high strength and good electrical conductivity compared with s-block metals.

Transition element or d-block element? AHL

DefinitionA transition element is an element whose atom or a common ion has an incomplete (partially filled) d sublevel. A d-block element is any element whose highest-energy electron is in a d sublevel.
  • Scandium is d-block but not usually counted as a transition element. Its only ion, Sc³⁺, is [Ar] with no d electrons.
  • Zinc is d-block but not a transition element. Zn is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s² and its only ion, Zn²⁺, is [Ar]3d¹⁰. The d sublevel is full and Zn has no variable oxidation states.

Why is zinc a d-block element but not a transition element?

  1. It has no electrons in a d sublevel
  2. It is in the p-block
  3. Its ion is Zn⁺, which has 4s¹
  4. Its only ion, Zn²⁺, has a full 3d¹⁰ sublevel

Zn²⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰: the d sublevel is complete, so neither the atom nor its common ion has a partially filled d sublevel.

Electron configurations of the first-row d-block

  • Recall the exceptions from S1.3: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (a half-full or full d sublevel is extra stable).
  • All of the first-row d-block atoms have electrons in the 4s sublevel.
  • When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are removed first, then 3d. For example, Fe [Ar]3d⁶4s² → Fe²⁺ [Ar]3d⁶ → Fe³⁺ [Ar]3d⁵. Cu⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰.

How many unpaired electrons does Mn²⁺ have?

Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s². Remove the two 4s electrons first: Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. By Hund's rule the five electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly, so there are 5 unpaired electrons.

Why transition metals have such strong metallic bonds AHL

Key pointIn transition elements the 3d and 4s sublevels are very close in energy, so both the 4s and the 3d electrons can become delocalized. More delocalized electrons per atom, together with small, highly charged cations, give stronger metallic bonding. This explains their higher melting points, and more charge carriers gives good electrical conductivity.

The strength of a metallic bond depends on three things: the number of delocalized electrons from each atom, the charge on the cation, and the size of the cation. Transition elements do well on all three. More delocalized electrons means each cation carries a higher effective charge and holds the electron sea more tightly, in effect behaving like a smaller, more highly charged ion.

Propertys-block metal (e.g. K, Ca)Transition metal (e.g. Fe, Cr)
Melting pointLow to moderate (K 63 °C; Ca 842 °C)High (Fe 1538 °C; Cr 1907 °C; W 3422 °C)
DensityLow (K 0.89 g cm⁻³)High (Fe 7.87 g cm⁻³)
Delocalized electronsOnly s electrons (1 or 2)4s and 3d electrons
Hardness/strengthSoft (group 1 can be cut with a knife)Hard and strong
Compare s-block and transition metals for (1) melting point and (2) density. Write your answer, then reveal the class model answer

Which statement best explains why iron has a much higher melting point than potassium?

  1. Iron atoms are heavier, so they need more energy to move
  2. Iron delocalizes both 4s and 3d electrons, and its cations are smaller and more highly charged
  3. Iron has covalent bonds between its atoms
  4. Potassium has London forces between its atoms

Melting point depends on the strength of the metallic bond, not on atomic mass. Fe delocalizes more electrons per atom and forms small, highly charged cations, so the electrostatic attraction is much stronger.

Link to S3.1The other characteristic properties of transition elements are studied in S3.1 (AHL): variable oxidation states (successive ionization energies rise gradually because 3d and 4s are close in energy, unlike group 1 where the 2nd electron comes from a much lower level), coloured complexes (d-orbital splitting), catalytic activity, and magnetic properties. Ions with unpaired d electrons, such as Fe²⁺ (3d⁶, 4 unpaired) and Fe³⁺ (3d⁵, 5 unpaired), are paramagnetic. Ions with all electrons paired, such as Zn²⁺, Cu⁺ and Sc³⁺, are diamagnetic.
Task: answer the guiding question "What determines the metallic nature and properties of an element?" in 3–4 sentences, then reveal

Elements with low ionization energy and low electronegativity lose their valence electrons easily, so in the solid they form a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalized electrons. The mobile electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity and lustre, and the non-directional attraction explains malleability and ductility. The strength of the bond, and so the melting point, depends on the charge and size of the cation and on the number of delocalized electrons; transition metals, which delocalize 3d as well as 4s electrons, have the strongest metallic bonding.
